column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

The article's 'one file-making expert' is read as a metalworker, as the article explains (metal parts such as the pagoda spire). Left out the World Heritage registration of July 2026 and the statue's height/gold details (King Daeheung of 'Goryeo' looks anachronistic).
The article contradicts itself on the birth year: the lead gives 30 October 1919, the body 30 October 1916 (the entry has 1916). The birth date is left out of the text.
Left out the article's garbled account of Octavian denying a fourth winner the honour and the debate over Cossus's rank (the entry mentions the debate).

The article says nearly a thousand inscriptions were found (and elsewhere 'hundreds'); the entry says hundreds, so no figure is given. 'Later work' for the AFSM courtyard excavation: the article does not date it.

Ayaz Kala 2: the article dates the fortress to the 6th-8th century CE but its palace to the 4th century CE; no date for it is given in the text. The 8th century also goes beyond the entry's 7th century.

The article contradicts itself on the founding (1803; Mallam Zaki appointed in early 1814; 'ruled from 1807 to 1914'), so no founding date or reign for Mallam Zaki is given. It also contradicts itself on whether Azare is the headquarters of Katagum LGA or of Zaki LGA: left out.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance, and its reign (c. 48/47-25 BCE) and era dates (58 or about 45 BC) disagree with the entry's r. c. 58-35 BCE and about 57 BCE
Gagik I given with no dates: the article marks his dates (989-1020) with an asterisk and calls him a king who campaigned against Syunik.
The article gives his death as c. 1187 or 1186/1188; written as 'probably died there in 1187' as the article's body has it, matching the entry's d. c. 1187.

The entry calls him a vassal of Hungary; the article says Kinnamos calls him an ally and that current scholarship sees him as an ally, not a vassal (while also calling him 'Hungarian vassal'). Worded as a disagreement among historians, without taking a side.
The article calls him the second son of Si Inthrathit (the eldest died as a child); the entry calls him the elder son. Neither ordinal is printed.

The article dates the destruction to about 613 and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's account to 607; the entry has the Battle of Chester around 615, so no date for the battle is given. The article also calls the monastery important in the 5th and 6th centuries though founded about 560: left out. The meeting with Augustine is not in the article.
The entry dates the Fatimid defeat of the alliance to 1029; the article gives only the rebellion of 1024-1025 and not its end, so no end date is given.
The article calls Yathill the capital of the Minaean kingdom at its peak (about 400 BCE) before the capital moved to Qarnāwu; the entry calls it the second city of Ma'in. Its rank is left out.
SKIPPED: article has well under 250 words of substance beyond a list of people born there
The Ziwiye burial named in the entry is not in the article.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; it does not give the day of the battle (only Constantine V's departure on 16 June 763), so little can be added to the entry
The article gives the date as 'about 8 January' and calls the dates approximate; the entry gives 8 January 871. The text explains how the date is derived without contradicting it.

The entry calls the Bhonsle chief 'the Bhonsle of Nagpur'; the article names him Raghoji II Bhonsle, Raja of Berar. Not contradictory. The article spells the river both Kaitna and Kailna; I used Kaitna.

Date: the entry says c. 1202; the article says the date is debated, Ibn Bibi gives 598 AH (1 October 1201 - 19 September 1202), and recent scholarship favours 1203 or 1204 (range 1202-1206). Left the date out. Command: the entry says the army fought under the Zakarid brothers; the article says it advanced under the command of David Soslan, with Zakaria and Ivane Mkhargrdzeli among his officers. I listed them together as commanders without saying who led overall, and kept Soslan only for the flank attack, which the article gives him.
The entry describes Sture's side as peasants, miners and burghers; the article names his support among the peasantry, Stockholm and Bergslagen. Consistent.

Length of the halt: the entry says the attack stalled the allied advance for more than a year; the article says the offensive was halted for ten months, until July 1867. Left the duration out. The article says 'the joint force of Brazilian, Argentine, and Uruguayan armies' but also that the troops involved in the attack were Brazilian and Argentine; I named the three allies only as the alliance. The article's naming of Marshal Osório as the Brazilian commander whose replacement was demanded looks doubtful (it also mentions Caxias resigning); left both out.

The article says Beornwulf's attack on Wessex came 'two years' after Ceolwulf's accession in 821, which does not fit 825; left the timing out. The entry lists Surrey among the kingdoms that submitted; the article names Sussex, Kent and Essex only, so I named those without denying Surrey. The article's paragraph on the Chronicle (written 890 CE, eyewitness accounts) is garbled; I used only the bare fact that it is the main source.

The article is short (about 500 words); two sections. The entry's statement that the order was dissolved within two years is not in the article and is not repeated. The article spells the land marshal Philipp/Philip von Bell/Belle; I used the entry's Philipp Schall von Bell.

Place of Müntzer's execution: the entry says near Mühlhausen, the article at Mühlhausen; left the place out and gave only the date. The article dates the battle 14-15 May; the entry 15 May, which is the day of the main fighting, so no conflict. The article calls the painting the world's largest oil painting; left that ranking out.

The article's lead says the battle was between Sparta and Athens and that Sparta was defeated by Athenians and Boeotians; its body describes Lysander's defeat by the Thebans before any Athenian force is mentioned. Followed the body and the entry (Thebans and the defenders).

Location: the entry says the battle was probably fought near the Cephissus in Boeotia; the article says recent scholarship, chiefly on the evidence of Marino Sanudo's 1327 letter, accepts Halmyros in southern Thessaly, and that the Cephissus was the older view (Muntaner, Gregoras, William Miller). Left the location out entirely. The flooded marsh: the entry states it as fact; the article gives it as Gregoras's account, commonly accepted, but notes the Chronicle of the Morea implies a hard fight and David Jacoby thinks the artificial marsh possibly invented on the model of the Battle of the Golden Spurs. I said only that the Catalans stood behind a swamp and the charge failed, and did not repeat or dispute the flooding.
The article gives Napoleon's arrival at Frankfurt both as the afternoon of 31 October and as the French reaching Frankfurt on 2 November; left the date out.

The article's lead dates the battle to June 49 BC; the entry gives the campaign as June to August. The surrender date is not given in the article beyond the encirclement by 30 July. Casualty figures are from Caesar's own account, quoted in the article.

The article calls Béla Ottokar's cousin; left that out as doubtful. It calls the battle one of the biggest in medieval Central Europe; left that ranking out. The entry places the battle on the March (Morava) east of Vienna; the article near Groissenbrunn in Lower Austria; consistent.
The entry says Majuba became a rallying cry for both sides; the article mentions only the British 'Remember Majuba'. I gave only the British cry without denying the other.

The article calls Marwan's side the Kalb-dominated Yaman confederation; the entry says the Kalb tribes; consistent. Numbers left out as the traditions disagree (6,000; 13,000 against 30,000; 30,000 against 60,000).
The article names the two scholars 'Lie Hounan' (刘俊男, which reads Liu Junnan) and Wang Fengfu; the romanisation looks garbled, so their names are left out.

The article says both sides claimed victory; the entry calls it a French victory. I said only that the French held the field. The article says William of Jülich commanded the force the French marched against but does not name him as commander at the battle itself; kept the article's wording.
SKIPPED: article has about 300 words, almost none on the battle itself; what it adds (Nájera, the Black Prince's withdrawal, du Guesclin made Duke of Molina) is too little for a longer text
The article dates the battle to September 190 BC; the entry gives 190 BCE. The article's claim that the battle secured Roman control of the Mediterranean for six centuries is left out.
The article's prelude dates Pelopidas's setting out to 376 BC while dating the battle to 375 BC; the year of the expedition is left out.
The entry places the battle near Péronne; the article says at Tertry, Somme. Both kept compatible by naming the Somme.

The article says the battle halted Muslim expansion for a decade or a generation; the entry says it weakened Umayyad power for several years. The duration is not stated; the dated recovery of 739-741 is given instead.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance; it adds only his parentage and an alliance with Amasis to what the entry already says

The entry says the temple collapsed, probably in an earthquake; the article gives an earthquake or the removal of its stone as possible causes. The cause is left out of the text; consider whether the entry's 'probably' should be softened.

The article dates a cistern inscription of the donor Vihnudata to the 2nd century AD while the other inscriptions are 2nd century BC; that date is left out. The article's claim that the carving disproves a foreign origin of the tabla is not repeated.

The entry names the 1832-1833 rising under Ganga Narayan Singh; the article's rebellion section covers the Chuar revolt and lists Ganga Narayan only among its supporters, so the 1832 rising is not retold.
The entry mentions Pokuttya; the article does not name the region, so the Polish war is told without it.

The article dates his death and the coup to 780; the entry gives 779. The year of the coup is left out (Daizong's death in 779 is kept). The article dates his conversion and the declaration of a state religion to 763; the entry says 762. The year is left out.

The article gives his birth as ca. 1253/58; the entry gives c. 1251. Birth year left out. The entry says he was briefly Duke of Kraków in 1288; the article has him take Kraków in 1288 and enter it again in summer 1289. Both are told as events; check whether the entry's date should read 1288-1289.
The article dates his wedding to Margareta both to 1308 and to 1318; the year is left out.
Benefit amounts are left out: the article gives them as current without a date.
The entry says he extended his power over Umbria and the Marche; the article's lead says Umbria and Lazio. Neither region list is repeated beyond Umbria.

The article dates the monastery's foundation to about 676; the entry says around 675. The year is left out of the text. Medeshamstede and the date of the friezes are not in the article and are not repeated.
The article dates the Council of Arles both 314 and 315; no year is given in the text.

The article spells the usurper Alectus and dates the Verona List 313–314 (the Britannia Prima article says c. 312); neither the name nor the date is given here. The article's account of the 296 invasion confuses Carausius with the invader and is not followed in detail.
The article says the brotherhood was registered in Hamburg in 1961 and survives there; the entry says it existed until 1940. The Hamburg revival is left out of the text.

The article gives his death as 24 February 1377 in its lead but 'about 1380' later; the death year is left out of the text (the entry has d. 1377). Whose wife Gangambika was is ambiguous in the article (most likely Kumara Kampana's); the text names her only as the author.
Rangoon date: the article says the Japanese forces reached Rangoon on 8 March.

The article puts the peak of 2.1 million barrels per day in 2004 in its lead but in 2003 in its production history; no year is given for the peak in the text (the entry says 2004). The entry's start of production in 1979 is not in the article.
The article gives 276 as the initial official count and 277 from the Minister of Defence and a congressional commission; only the first is used.
Greek writers' link of the Carians with the Leleges and the Old Testament references were left out for length.

The article numbers his father Mieszko I Tanglefoot; the entry has Mieszko IV Tanglefoot. The text gives no numeral. The article says some historians put his death a year earlier; the entry gives 1230, as the article's main date does. The new castle at Opole named in the entry is not in the article.
The 1230 inscription of Chandrabhanu named in the entry is not in the article. The article's claim that the temples stored rice because of the Japanese invasion is unclear and was left out.
The Province of Queen Adelaide named in the entry is not in the article.
The article is short (about 300 words); the text uses nearly all of it.

The article gives 140,806 speakers in the 2000 census and also an estimated 120,000 speakers, and says most Chʼol are monolingual while the census counts 40,000 monolinguals; the figures are left out. The entry's Lacandon and Manche Chʼol of Guatemala, who resisted into the late 17th century, are not in the article; the text speaks of the Chʼol sent north in the 1550s, whom the article calls the ancestors of today's Chʼol.
The entry's years as a teacher in Kyoto are not in the article.
The article calls him privy counsellor of Christian Augustus; the entry calls him chancellor. The text names no office.

The article's lead puts the climax at Cetinje on 7 January 1919 (Orthodox Christmas), while its narrative puts the battle on 6 January; I gave only the 6 January figures from the narrative and did not date a climax. Entry says guerrilla resistance continued for several years; article: until 1929. Compatible.
The article is short (about 380 words); two sections only. The entry says the chronicle covers events up to 1326; the addendum to 1330 is mentioned as the article gives it.
The article says Kim Ch'ont'aek was a 'Pogyo constable'; I wrote constable only, as the term is not explained.

The entry says Abu Sa'id came to the throne in 1317; the article says Öljeitü died in 1316 and Abu Sa'id then confirmed Chupan. I gave no year for the accession. The article dates Chupan's betrothal to Sati Beg both to 1317 and 'since 1316'; I gave no year. Death given as October/November 1327 in the article lead; I wrote only that he was killed, after 25 August 1327, without a month.

The article's lead gives construction as 1398-1515, while its construction section says the tower was finished in 1544; I left the end of construction out. The article speaks of King Rupert and of Elector Ruprecht/Rupert III as founder; these are the same man. The sentence on Brian Clarke's windows is garbled in the article ('Ultimately, of Clarke's designs were implemented'), so I left Clarke out.

The article gives his dates as 5th century - c. 530 in its lead but reports wide scholarly disagreement (one annal source via O'Halloran gives birth in 352); I gave no dates. I left out the miracle story concerning the nun Bruinnech and the modern dispute about it.

SKIPPED: The article has about 300 words, adds little beyond the entry, and its dates (power c. 365 BC, death 353 BC) differ from the entry's (364 and 352 BCE); it also names Chion, the assassin, not Clearchus, as the pupil of Plato and Isocrates.

The entry speaks of large bronze arrowhead hoards; the article's archaeology section mentions only eight arrowheads in the drum hoard. I did not mention hoards of arrowheads. Kim's population estimate (5,000-10,000) left out.

The entry calls Codelco the world's largest copper producer; the article says it is the largest copper mining company but was the second largest producer in 2025. I gave no ranking. The entry's 1958 law and its 2019 repeal are not in the article; the article mentions a 10% tax on foreign currency sales (Law 13,196). Left out. The 2026 allegation of inflated 2025 production figures left out.

The article says both that the city became capital of Germania Inferior at its promotion around 50 and that the province was founded under Domitian in 89, the city becoming capital 'ten years' after 80; I gave no date for it becoming capital.
The article names Yeltsin's post both as Chairman of the Supreme Soviet and of the Presidium; I wrote 'chairman'.

The entry says Metternich called the congress; the article says it met at the behest of Tsar Alexander I. I did not say who called it. The entry calls it a conference of the Holy Alliance; the article of the Quintuple Alliance. I named neither.
Article says Quebec's government passed a resolution authorizing an amendment 15 years later; left out. The Quebec point is kept to past facts, without 'as of'.

The entry says the council condemned more than a thousand people to death; the article (citing Jonathan Israel) says almost nine thousand were convicted, of whom only about 1,000 sentences were carried out. I gave only the nine thousand convicted and did not state the number executed.
The entry calls her a mother goddess; the article does not, but does not contradict it. I did not use the term.

The article's plot summary opens with an editorial passage on Danton and Robespierre ('slaughter uncounted thousands') that does not describe the play; I left it out. Plot of the first act is not given in the article.

Accession: the article gives 1382 in the lead but 'around 1379/80' in the body; the entry gives 1382. I gave no year. The death of Sa'ad ad-Din: al-Maqrizi 1402/03, the Walasma chronicle 1415 (under Yeshaq), Chekroun 1408/09; the entry says around 1410. I gave no year. A 2011 study of Zeila found no conclusive evidence of a siege. End of reign: the article gives 6 October 1413 but says most historians place it at 1411-1412; the entry gives 1413. I gave no year. The tradition of his death at the hands of Mansur ad-Din of Adal left out. The Egyptian campaign is dated 'around 1380' in the article, before the entry's accession date; I wrote 'early in his reign'.

The article dates the uprising August 209 B.C. to January 208 B.C.; the entry says crushed within months, consistent. The article says Chen was declared king of the former Kingdom of Chu; the entry names it Zhangchu, not in the article, so I wrote only what the article says.
The article mentions terms of vassalage agreed in 1242 but also says Vatatzes forced John's submission in 1244; I left the 1242 date out.

Death date uncertain in the article (1482, 1485, at least 1499; dead by 1502); left out, as the entry gives c. 1500. The entry names the kingdom of Kantora; the article only names the market town of Cantor.

Entry says conservatives backed by the federal president removed him; the article says the coup was led by Colonel Milla and aided by Honduran Conservatives, with no mention of the federal president. I wrote only what the article says. Comayagua as capital is not in the article.
The article gives no exact date for the Senate speech; the entry says around 61 BCE, so I gave no year. Delamarre's first name is not in the article.
The entry dates the fort to around 1552; the article gives no year, so none is given. Hrushevsky's first name is not in the article: removing if flagged.
The article does not mention the Asen revolt by name; the entry's link to it was not repeated. The article says he died after 1201 without a date; I wrote only that he disappears from the sources.

The article dates Lysimachus's capture variously between 294 and 291 BCE; the entry says about 292 BCE, consistent, so no year given. The article places his kingdom on both sides of the lower Danube; the entry says north of it. I did not state the extent.

The article dates the move of the Kaan seat to Calakmul both to around 580-590 (History section) and to 636 (lead); the entry says the 7th century. I left the date of the move out. The article's lead calls Dzibanche the most powerful Maya city of the region; not repeated as a ranking.
The article's lead says he was found guilty and imprisoned in 1827, while its abduction section says he was brought to trial in 1826; the entry gives no year, so none is given here.
Brecht's words are in copyright; the Contents section describes their theme in our own words and quotes no line.

The article dates his death and the end of his reign to 1610/11; the entry says about 1610, so no year is given here. The article places the English arrival of 1612 and Anaukpetlun's invasion of 1613-1614 in his reign, which contradicts its own dates for the reign; both left out.

The article says she was sentenced to death on 20 August 1799 and also gives 20 August as her death date; I did not give a day for the hanging. Of eight other patriots sentenced, she was the last to be hanged: I wrote the last of nine, which is the article's count plus her.

The article's plague figure (over 900,000 bodies every 50 days) is left out as implausible without a second source. The article's spelling is Rashid-al-Din Hamadani; check the checker on 'Rashid al-Din'.
The entry's Rouran raid after his death is not in the article; nothing written about it.
Recent sponsorship and the 2025-2026 changes left out as not lasting. The article says the race moved to Saturday after 1994 and also that it moved in 1995; I left the change of day out.
The article says Erling's allies drove Olav out after the killing; I kept its wording.
Death toll: the article gives an estimate of 10,000 to 980,000 and Amnesty International's figure of up to 500,000; the entry says tens of thousands. The overall toll is left out of the text.
The article gives his death date as 13 April 1874 in the lead and says he was executed; I combined the two, which the article implies but does not state outright.

The article says that in 1298, after her husband's death, she returned to her brother's court at Constantinople with her son Michael and came back to Trebizond only in 1301; the entry says she remained influential at her son's court from John's death in 1297 until her own. The text leaves out where she lived between 1298 and 1301. The article names the inscription's recorder by surname only (Fallmerayer).

The 'Sabaean translation' given in the article names Kaleb, Ella Atsbeha, son of Tazena, and invokes Christ and the Trinity: it appears to be a later inscription of King Kaleb, not Ezana's, so it was left out of the contents. The article states the conquest of Meroë both as part of the stone's content and as a campaign around 350; the text keeps to the campaign.

The article does not say how Otto I or Hermann II were related to Ezzo, so no relationships were stated. The article lists Carinthia among the duchies held; the entry names only Swabia and Bavaria, which does not contradict it.
The entry says Felixstowe commemorates him; the article says Felixstowe may have been named after him, with 'the stow of Filica' as an alternative. The text does not discuss the name.

The article does not give the year 677 BCE, Yong's tombs or Li Maozhen, all of which the entry has; it names the Qi Kingdom (907–924) without its ruler. Climate, population (as of 2004) and economic figures left out.
The article dates the monastery to 598; the entry says around 600. The text gives no founding year.

The article's chronology is confused: it dates his independence to 1603 and the 1605 battles, then says he went to Goa 'the next year' and returned in 1602. The text gives no year for the Goa journey. The entry says he made himself independent 'with support from Portuguese Goa'; the article speaks only of recognition and titles from the Portuguese court.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance: myth, literary mentions and papyrus only, no history beyond the entry

The entry calls him a naval officer; the article says he was discharged in 1763 without being commissioned as an officer. The text says only that he left the navy. The article says King Rama II of Siam thwarted the 1785 proposal that Light become governor of Thalang; Rama II did not reign in 1785, so the episode was left out.
The article gives his death as 28 October 1816 in the lead and the execution as 29 October 1816 in the body; the text gives no day.
The article says that after his wife's death (1842) he retired to private life, which conflicts with its own account of his offices up to 1848; the retirement is left out.

The article gives his birth as c. 1615 or 1620; the entry has c. 1615. The text gives no birth year. The article's section 'Inheritance in Batavia' gives dates (1704, 1736, 1762) that cannot belong to this Coyett and seems to mix him with a later namesake; it was left out.

The article says Rudolf also granted him 'the rank of a Prince-Elector'; this is doubtful and was left out. The article dates John I c. 1279, before the second marriage of 10 April 1280; no birth years of the children are given.
The article gives his work as 'Die Volkserhebung in Baden' in the text and as 'Die Erhebung des Volkes in Baden für die deutsche Republik' in its list of works; the text uses the first.
Short article (about 300 words); two sections.
The entry says the fort was built probably under Harald Bluetooth; the article says it was likely built under Harald Gormsson or his son Sweyn Forkbeard. The text names no builder.

The article's lead gives 3 September 1540 for his accession and its section 2 September 1540; only the month is given here. The article says 'Vizier Abbas' was killed with his captains and later that an 'Abbas, one of the principal figures of Adal' was captured in 1549; only the first is mentioned.

The article contradicts itself on his birth: 29 May 556 in its lead, 557 in its Background section; no birth year is given here. The article dates his death c. November 577 (winter 577); the entry's dates end in 578. No year of death is given here ('Later').
The Vieira estimate of disease deaths (1615-1652) was left out: the article's quotation is unclosed and its 1842 date for Antonio Vieira looks doubtful.

SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance: beyond the entry it gives only his parentage, his marriage to Anna of Sweden and a list of children The entry says Count Palatine of Veldenz and Lützelstein from 1544; the article says he obtained Lützelstein only in 1553.
The article's 2010 census figures were left out as dated statistics.
The article calls him a 'teacher' after becoming contador, which seems a slip; left out.
The article dates the Teatro Farnese 1618-1628; the entry says built in 1618. No date for the theatre is given here.
Left out the article's 'As of 2026' claim that he remains the oldest verified head of state in office.

The entry says he took Angelokastron and Lepanto after 1359; the article dates his conquest of Nafpaktos (Lepanto) to 1376 or 1377. No date for his first taking of Nafpaktos is given here. The article says Schiró found Shpata had only daughters, yet also that his son succeeded him; the son is mentioned as the article's death section has it, Schiró's view on sons left out. The article's Possessions list dates Arta 1375-99 against 1374 in its text; the text's 1374 (also the entry's) is used.
The article gives both 375 BC and 388 BC for the Gallic invasion that ended the culture; only the century is given here.

The article dates the three main Gond kingdoms 14th to 18th centuries; the entry says 16th to 18th. No start date is given here. Left out the article's unsourced claim that the Gond are the progenitors of all Kshatriyas, and the present-day political parties.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance and adds little to the entry beyond his father Gongsun Kang and his uncle Gongsun Gong
The article's 'As of 2006' description (hotel, eatery) was left out except the lasting facts.
The article contradicts itself on Drogo's wife Gaitelgrima: Guaimar's sister in the Hauteville section, his younger daughter in the Family section. Left out.
The article excerpt says nothing of his marriage beyond Lady Chai's advice and nothing of the events of 950 in Kaifeng; the sons' death date is from its family list.
The article gives two totals of successful Joseon candidates in the highest examinations: 'more than 14,606' in its overview and 14,620 in its literary section; neither is used.
The article gives Tang forces of 144,000; kept as the article has it. Two sections only: the article has little beyond the last battle.

The entry says Harald made him earl of Trøndelag; the article says he was made earl of Sunnfjord and Nordfjord (and later given Fjordane). His earldom's name left out of the text. The entry places him in Hålogaland; the article does not say so.

The article dates the wars from 133 BCE (the failed ambush at Mayi) and the first offensive from late 129 BCE; the entry dates the war from 129 BCE. The text gives Mayi as background without calling it the start of the war.
The article gives Zongzhou as another name of Hao itself; the entry gives it to the royal centre of both settlements. Worded so as not to decide between them.
241 words: the article has about 270 words in all and every fact in it is used; not padded to 260.

The entry glosses Buzurg as 'Hasan the Tall'; the article as 'Hasan the Great'. No gloss given in the text. The entry says Chupanids; the text follows the article's 'Chobanids' for the faction (Chupan for the man).

The entry dates the first capture of Carthage to 695; the article says he entered Ifriqiya in 692/93, 693/94 or 695 and gives no year for the first capture. No year given in the text. The article contradicts itself on the destruction of Carthage (698, then 'upon his approach' after al-Kahina's death, 'in 698'). Only the 698 recapture and destruction is told. The entry calls the queen Dihya; the article al-Kahina. The text uses al-Kahina.
The entry dates the war with Russia 1741–1743; the article gives no years for it beyond the Treaty of Åbo (1743). No years given for the war in the text.
The article dates her death c. 50–56 CE; the entry d. c. 50 CE. No death date given in the text.
The entry says he took Chang'an in 418; the article tells the capture under the Jin events of 417 without a clear year for his entry into the city. No year given for the capture in the text.

The article contradicts itself on his Malabar command (lead: governor 1669–1676; body: appointed commander 1670, moved to Batavia in 1677) and on the number of plants (740 in the lead, 742 in the body). Neither the years of command nor the number of plants is given in the text; the entry's 1670–1677 is not contradicted.

The entry says the Great Garden was laid out from 1666; the article gives 1666 as the founding of the Hill Garden (as a vegetable garden) and 1683 as Sophia's commission to enlarge the existing Great Garden. 1666 is given only for the Hill Garden, as the article has it; no founding year for the Great Garden.

The article dates the destruction of the mudbrick wall 'around 530 BC'; the entry says 530 BCE. No year given in the text. The text says the mudbrick wall was 'burned' from the article's 'fiery destruction'.

The article gives his birth as 20 February 1822 in the lead and 18 February 1822 in the body; no birth day given in the text. The entry's postal service and newspapers are not in the article; not repeated.

The article gives the first patient as received on 1 January 1452 and the consecration as 31 December 1452, which do not sit well together; neither date given in the text. The article calls the work one of the finest examples of 15th-century Burgundian architecture and the façade Northern Renaissance; the entry says late Gothic. No style named in the text.

The entry says Guy became Count of Flanders in 1278; the article lists him as count jure matris from 1251 and in his own right from 1280. No year given for his Flemish title in the text. The entry has the Flemish line pass by Margaret III's marriage in 1369; the article has the senior line end at her death in 1405. Both told without contradiction: her death and succession are given, not a date of passing.
